title: Exercise 7B · Q9
summary: Find BQ in ΔQKB, then PB, then HB in ΔPHB, and finally HK.
alt: Exercise 7B · Q9: Two spotlights, P and Q, are mounted on a vertical pole AB. Light beams from P and Q shine to two points on the ground, H and K, respectively. Given that PQ = 12.7 m, KB = 17.2 m, PH = 39 m and QK = 21 m, find (i) BQ, the height above the ground at which the spotlight Q is mounted, (ii) HK, the distance between the projections of the light beams.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: Spotlights **P** and **Q** are mounted on a vertical pole **AB** (foot **B**). Beams **PH** and **QK** shine to ground points **H** and **K**. **PQ = 12.7 m**, **KB = 17.2 m**, **PH = 39 m**, **QK = 21 m**. Find (i) **BQ**, (ii) **HK**.

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔQKB, **∠B = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **QK**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{QK^2} &= \role{legA}{KB^2} + \role{legB}{BQ^2} \\ \role{legB}{BQ^2} &= \role{hyp}{QK^2} - \role{legA}{KB^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{QK^2} &= \role{legA}{KB^2} + \role{legB}{BQ^2} \\ \role{legB}{BQ^2} &= \role{hyp}{QK^2} - \role{legA}{KB^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{21^2} - \role{legA}{17.2^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{441} - \role{legA}{295.84} \\ &= \role{legB}{145.16}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 145.16 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{QK^2} &= \role{legA}{KB^2} + \role{legB}{BQ^2} \\ \role{legB}{BQ^2} &= \role{hyp}{QK^2} - \role{legA}{KB^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{21^2} - \role{legA}{17.2^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{441} - \role{legA}{295.84} \\ &= \role{legB}{145.16} \\ \role{legB}{BQ} &= \sqrt{145.16} = \role{ans}{12.0\ \text{m}}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Find PB
steps.narration: **PB** is the whole pole segment from **P** down to **B**: add **PQ** and **BQ**.\[\begin{aligned}PB &= PQ + QB \\ &= 12.7 + 12.05 = 24.75\ \text{m}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔPHB, **∠B = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **PH**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides. We want a shorter side, so subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PH^2} &= \role{legA}{HB^2} + \role{legB}{PB^2} \\ \role{legA}{HB^2} &= \role{hyp}{PH^2} - \role{legB}{PB^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and subtract
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and subtract.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PH^2} &= \role{legA}{HB^2} + \role{legB}{PB^2} \\ \role{legA}{HB^2} &= \role{hyp}{PH^2} - \role{legB}{PB^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{39^2} - \role{legB}{24.75^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1521} - \role{legB}{612.56} \\ &= \role{legA}{908.44}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 908.44 is not a perfect square. Use a calculator and keep 4 significant figures — we need this value again.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{PH^2} &= \role{legA}{HB^2} + \role{legB}{PB^2} \\ \role{legA}{HB^2} &= \role{hyp}{PH^2} - \role{legB}{PB^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{39^2} - \role{legB}{24.75^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1521} - \role{legB}{612.56} \\ &= \role{legA}{908.44} \\ \role{legA}{HB} &= \sqrt{908.44} = 30.14\ \text{m}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: (ii) Find HK
steps.narration: **HK** is what is left of **HB** after taking away **KB**.\[\begin{aligned}HK &= HB - KB \\ &= 30.14 - 17.2 = \role{ans}{12.9\ \text{m}}\ \text{(3 s.f.)}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Check PB
challenges.prompt: PQ = 12.7 m and BQ = 12.05 m. Find PB.

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.

notes.title: Rounding
notes.text: If the answer is not a whole number, give it to **3 significant figures** unless the question says otherwise.
